Precision Agriculture: Herbicide Reduction with AI Models
documents.abstract: Extended Abstract Sugarcane cultivation has been concentrated in several countries due to its diversity of use, such as in fuel, sugar, as well as other areas. Among the 80 largest sugarcane producers, Brazil occupies the first place, representing 22% of world production in the 2020/2021 harvest. The modernization of agriculture, called agriculture 4.0, has allowed greater productivity, which are directly affected by the invasion of weeds. A survey presented by [1] shows that the invasion of Brachiaria decumbens and Panicum (weed varieties) were responsible for the loss of 40% of the sugarcane production. Integrated weed management, which includes constant mapping in a crop and the appropriate choice of control strategies, can be achieved through a better understanding of the structure and production system in relation to the behaviour of weeds in the field, as well as the optimization of its control. The adoption of the soil mapping method in the regular network allows producers, who use the localized application of fertilizers and herbicides, to make agribusiness more competitive and efficient in agricultural management and in increasing productivity [2]. In a study carried out by [3] it was observed that with the application of targeted herbicide (punctually) in beet, corn, wheat and others cultivars, it was possible to obtain a reduction from 6 to 81% in applications directed to weeds of broad-leaved and a 20 to 79% reduction in applications targeting narrow-leaf weeds. In this survey, we propose a supervised machine learning model, which was able to identify weed invasion in a sugarcane cultivar, using four colour spectra as input variables, being NIR, RE, R and G, which were obtained by a multispectral camera adapted to an unmanned aerial vehicle. documents.title: Smart agriculture framework from imagery based on representation learning
Patch-To-Prediction: Vision Transformers for Weed Detection in Real-World Farming Conditions
documents.abstract: Weeds reduce crop yields, raise production costs, and therefore minimize the opportunity for sustainable agricultural practices. Consequently, it is essential to identify weeds promptly and accurately. As a long-standing and traditional endeavor, manual weed detection is labor-intensive, slow, and prone to possible errors. Earlier automated approaches primarily employed classical image processing techniques, which relied mainly on color, texture, or shape. Nevertheless, these methods struggle when crops and weeds look similar or when there is a visually complex background. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely used in fashion weed detection, they rely on having a large dataset for model training. Even then, they have been less successful when data is limited. To address these concerns, we propose a weed identification system that utilizes the Vision Transformer (ViT). Based on an architecture that divides an image into patches, it applies self-attention to realize the global contextual relationships. It realizes a more accurate classification of regions when weeds visually resemble the crop and/or when weed features are occluded. Our system utilizes non-specialized RGB images captured at ground level with a mobile device or a field camera, thereby eliminating the need for a drone or specialized mapping equipment. By using transfer learning with a pre-trained Transformer model, the system achieves higher identification accuracy rates than less accurate methods, usually as data limitation declines.

documents.title: Modular Transformer Architecture for Precision Agriculture Imaging
documents.abstract: This paper addresses the critical need for efficient and accurate weed segmentation from drone video in precision agriculture. A quality-aware modular deep-learning framework is proposed that addresses common image degradation by analyzing quality conditions-such as blur and noise-and routing inputs through specialized pre-processing and transformer models optimized for each degradation type. The system first analyzes drone images for noise and blur using Mean Absolute Deviation and the Laplacian. Data is then dynamically routed to one of three vision transformer models: a baseline for clean images, a modified transformer with Fisher Vector encoding for noise reduction, or another with an unrolled Lucy-Richardson decoder to correct blur. This novel routing strategy allows the system to outperform existing CNN-based methods in both segmentation quality and computational efficiency, demonstrating a significant advancement in deep-learning applications for agriculture.

documents.title: CRowNet: Deep Network for Crop Row Detection in UAV Images
documents.abstract: Nowadays, the development of robots and smart tractors for the automation of sowing, harvesting, weeding etc. is transforming agriculture. Farmers are moving from an agriculture where everything is applied uniformly to a much more targeted farming. This new kind of farming is commonly referred to as precision agriculture. However for autonomous guidance of these agricultural machines and even sometimes for weed detection an accurate detection of crop rows is required. In this paper we propose a new method called CRowNet which uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) and the Hough transform to detect crop rows in images taken by an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The method consists of a model formed with SegNet (S-SegNet) and a CNN based Hough transform (HoughCNet). The performance of the proposed method was quantitatively compared to traditional approaches and it showed the best and most robust result. A good crop row detection rate of 93.58% was obtained with an $IoU$ score per crop row above 70%. Moreover the model trained on a given crop field is able to detect rows in images of different types of crops.

documents.title: On the Transferability of Agricultural Weed Detection Under Cross-Field Distribution Shift
documents.abstract: Accurate agricultural weed detection in real-world field conditions is essential for precision agriculture, enabling targeted intervention and reducing yield loss. Recent work has reported strong detection performance from UAV-based imagery across a range of crops, yet existing approaches evaluate within a single crop and field, leaving practitioners with little evidence that a model trained on one crop will generalize to a new field or crop type. In this work, we characterize where cross-dataset weed-localization performance degrades and which modeling choices recover it, reducing the need to relabel every new deployment field. We introduce a newly collected and annotated UAV image dataset for agricultural weed detection in cotton fields and use it alongside an existing soybean dataset collected under a similar protocol. Using these datasets, we evaluate the performance of several strategies for transferring a detector trained on one crop to another, comparing unsupervised domain adaptive object detection (DAOD) against pretraining on a domain-adjacent source dataset followed by few-shot fine-tuning on the target dataset. Our analysis spans target-domain label budgets from zero to the full target dataset, characterizing the trade-off between adaptation strategy and annotation effort. We find that few-shot fine-tuning with as few as 25 labeled target examples outperforms unsupervised DAOD in our cross-crop comparison, suggesting that source domain selection combined with modest target supervision is more productive than algorithmic sophistication in adaptation.

documents.title: LONG RANGE UNMANNED AERIAL VEHICLE FOR FORESTRY MONITORING USING LIDAR
Pest and Weed Detection Using Artificial Intelligence
documents.abstract: The project aims to develop an Artificial Intelligence system which automatically detects field pests and weeds with high accuracy. The contemporary agricultural sector requires smart sustainable solutions because of population growth and climate change and the increasing need to produce food worldwide. The traditional approach to pest and weed identification requires field workers to manually identify pests while using pesticides, which creates an inefficient method that harms the ecosystem. The proposed system uses image processing technology to address existing system weaknesses, while machine learning and deep learning techniques analyze drone and automated field robot crop images. Advanced deep learning models, in particular Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are able to detect subtle patterns and accurately classify infected areas - often being able to find problems where the human eye might not notice anything. The system uses agricultural image datasets to train and validate its performance, which allows it to operate successfully across multiple crop types and different agricultural environments. The system evaluates its performance through accuracy measurement and precision assessment, and recall testing, and F1-score evaluation. The model enables precise detection, which decreases unnecessary pesticide use, resulting in reduced operational expenses and supporting environmentally friendly agricultural practices. The AI system improves decision-making processes while enhancing crop production and developing sustainable agricultural methods that protect future food security needs.

documents.title: AI-Driven Robotic Inspection for Forest and Grassland Ecosystems: Progress, Framework and Challenges
documents.abstract: Forests and grasslands provide critical ecological services, yet they are confronted with various threats, including wildfire hazards, vegetation degradation, biological invasions, and pest and disease outbreaks. Conventional inspection methods, such as fixed-point observation, are constrained by sparse coverage and delayed reporting. In recent years, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) have been widely explored for image and video data collection during forest and grassland inspections. This review synthesizes recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-driven robotic inspection for forest and grassland ecosystems, organizing these developments into a comprehensive framework encompassing multi-source sensing, task-specific perception and understanding, and the corresponding outcomes. Three representative tasks are further elaborated: early wildfire detection for timely warning and intervention; vegetation assessment with a focus on canopy conditions, biomass, and vegetation coverage; and the identification of plant species, weeds, and pests. In these tasks, various AI models are selected for image recognition, with full consideration of deployment feasibility, response time, and performance accuracy. Furthermore, three key challenges in forest and grassland management are identified: regional decision-making, robotic mission planning and coordination, and operational performance evaluation in field intervention, with the goal of promoting sustainable ecological management.

documents.title: Automated Weed Classification Techniques: Datasets, Methods, and Challenges
documents.abstract: Automated weeding remains a prominent challenge in agriculture domain, and it needs to addressed effectively to improve the crop yield and quality. Traditional methods of weeding (herbicide treatments or manual removal) are often labor-intensive, not affordable, and the chemical control with herbicides causes soil pollution. Recent advancements in deep learning and computer vision techniques, however, have introduced a set of tools that are increasingly proving to be efficient, precise, and largely automated. In this review, we focus on literature sourced from the Stored Literature Collections database, surveying prior studies on state-of-the-art approaches, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), DenseNet architectures, transfer learning, attention mechanisms, and the explainable AI (XAI) framework, all applied to the classification and detection of weeds among cotton, sorghum, and maize crops. The widely employed benchmark weed datasets and its prominent characteristics are reported in the work. The state-of-the-art machine learning and deep learning algorithms employed in automated weeding systems are discussed in detail. The integration of these algorithms with robotics, UAVs, and precision agriculture systems enables minimizing chemical usage and boosting the sustainability of agricultural practices. The work also addresses the potential challenges and feasible solutions in implementing the automated weeding systems on edge devices.
